response.title: Are the cheap off-brand battery power stations good enough for home outage backup, or should I pay for a big name?
response.answer:
For home outage backup, I'd generally pay extra for a reputable brand—but not necessarily the most expensive one.

Cheap off-brand portable power stations can work perfectly well. The problem is that an outage backup system needs to be dependable after sitting unused for months, not just perform well when you first unbox it.

The biggest differences aren't always battery capacity or wattage. They're battery safety, inverter reliability, quality control, warranty support, and how the unit behaves when something goes wrong.

Where cheap power stations fall short

Price per Wh

	

Often excellent

	

Higher, especially at full price

A cheap unit isn't automatically unsafe, and a big-name unit isn't automatically reliable. The specific model matters much more than the logo.

What I'd actually buy

For most households, I'd target a 1,000–2,000Wh LiFePO4 (LFP) power station with at least 1,500W continuous AC output.

Here are two examples showing why buying a recognizable brand doesn't necessarily require spending a fortune.

B&H Photo

Another solid option with higher continuous output.

These are current listed prices, not guarantees of long-term reliability. At roughly $500–$550 for a branded 1kWh station, I'd need a substantial discount to justify taking a chance on an unknown manufacturer.

How much battery do you actually need?

Assuming 85% usable AC energy after inverter losses:

These are illustrative estimates. Refrigerator consumption varies significantly, and its compressor may require a much higher startup wattage.

My checklist for a cheap off-brand unit

I'd consider buying one only if it meets all of these:

LiFePO4 battery chemistry, rather than an unspecified lithium battery.

Verifiable independent safety certification, ideally UL 2743 or an applicable equivalent from an accredited testing lab—not merely a manufacturer's claim of being "UL compliant."

Pure sine wave inverter with enough continuous and surge power for the intended appliances.

Documented warranty and real customer support, including a credible way to obtain repairs or replacements.

Independent load testing demonstrating realistic usable capacity, inverter efficiency and thermal behavior.

UL Solutions distinguishes portable power packs certified under UL 2743 from stationary residential battery systems, which generally require UL 9540 certification. A portable station's certification alone doesn't make it suitable for permanent home electrical integration. 
UL Solutions
+1

For home backup, plug appliances directly into the station or use a properly installed, compatible transfer system. Never backfeed a household outlet.

My buying rule

I'd use these rough thresholds when comparing otherwise similar units:

Off-brand is 10–20% cheaper: Buy the established brand.

Off-brand is 30–40% cheaper: Consider it if safety certifications and independent testing check out.

Off-brand is 50%+ cheaper: Worth investigating, but be particularly skeptical of capacity and safety claims.

Portable battery banks, usually under $100, are convenient for phones, computers and lights but cannot run major appliances.
